## 4. lore — why 'evlo' swallowed its own middle

**ANNA:** why 'evlo' swallowed its own middle

**ANNA:** The word the textbook gives you is 'evvalavu' — how much, how many, how large.

**ANNA:** எவ்வளவு

**ANNA:** Four syllables. Nobody in Coimbatore has ever said all four in a real sentence.

**ANNA:** What happens in fast speech is the middle collapses. 'Evvalavu' loses its second and third syllable almost entirely — what survives is the front and the tail, pressed together.

**ANNA:** எவ்ளோ

**ANNA:** The 'lavu' — the part that meant 'measure', that gave the word its weight — is just gone. What's left is the question and the vowel that closes it. The meaning didn't shrink; only the shape did.

**ANNA:** And 'lama' — the permission word — does the same thing from the other direction. The full form is 'aaguma', meaning roughly 'will it become acceptable'. Asking the world if a thing is allowed to exist.

**ANNA:** ஆகுமா

**ANNA:** That softened over generations into 'lama'. The philosophy stayed — you are not demanding, you are asking whether the situation will permit — but the syllables quietly left.

## 10. lore — why -ணும் feels like gravity

**ANNA:** why -ணும் feels like gravity

**ANNA:** There is a word in Tamil that means something like want, or need, or wish — depending on who is saying it and how tired they are.

**ANNA:** வேணும்
> that word

**ANNA:** Coimbatore people dropped the middle of the classical form years ago and kept only the weight of it. What is left is not want exactly — it is closer to the pull a thing has on you. The thing wants to happen.

**ANNA:** When you fold it onto a verb, you are not adding a rule from outside. You are saying the action itself has that pull.

**ANNA:** போகணும்
> must go — the going is already pulling

**ANNA:** A machine has no choice about what it does next. The lever moves, the gear turns, the next thing happens. That is what -ணும் sounds like from inside a sentence — not a command from a person above, just the next thing that has to happen.

**ANNA:** சொல்லணும்
> must say — the saying is owed

**ANNA:** And then there is the other pair — the one about time. Tamil has two endings that English collapses into one word: going.

**ANNA:** போறேன்
> going — the wheel already turning

**ANNA:** போவேன்
> will go — the wheel not yet engaged

**ANNA:** The -உறேன் ending is a machine mid-cycle. Something is already in motion. The -வேன் ending is the machine before you throw the switch — the intention is there, the motion is not. Tamil heard this difference and decided it needed two separate sounds.

**ANNA:** English let it go. Tamil did not. That is the whole story.
